result: STS neurons show selectivity for specific combinations of head-body orientations, with significant interactions between head and body orientation demonstrated through two-way ANOVA analyses. A large fraction of neurons in both aSTS and mSTS showed significant interactions between head and body orientation across different centerings and poses, indicating that heads and bodies interact at the level of the STS.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. Reviewer 1 states the study shows 'different neurons showed preferences for body orientation, or head orientation or for the interaction between the two.' Reviewer 2 notes 'STS neurons integrate head and body information in a nonlinear way, showing selectivity for specific combinations of head-body orientations.' Reviewer 3 similarly confirms 'STS neurons integrate head and body information in a nonlinear way.' No concerns are raised about this fundamental result.

result: Anterior STS (aSTS) neurons enabled more reliable decoding of head-body configuration angles compared to middle STS (mSTS) neurons, with higher position tolerance. The median correlations between MC and HC were 0.68 for aSTS and 0.57 for mSTS (p=0.008), and residual correlations were significantly higher in aSTS (0.41) than mSTS (0.23, p=0.008), demonstrating position-tolerant head-body orientation interactions in aSTS but less so in mSTS.
evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirm this regional difference. Reviewer 1 notes the study shows 'the neuronal population can decode head-body angle presented across orientations, in the anterior aSTS patch (but not middle mSTS patch)' and that 'mSTS neurons show less invariance for head-body angle.' Reviewer 2 states 'Head-body configuration angles can be reliably decoded, particularly for neurons in the anterior STS, suggesting a transformation of face/body orientation signals from the middle to the anterior STS.' No methodological concerns are raised about these analyses.

result: Decoding accuracy in aSTS was highest for aligned (0°) versus straight (180°) head-body orientations and lowest for configurations differing only in sign (±90°). This pattern was robust across three experiments, with classification accuracy reaching ~0.7-0.9 for zero versus straight angles but near chance for left versus right angles. The confusion between mirror-symmetric configurations suggests the neuronal population is relatively insensitive to the sign of the angle.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this key finding. Reviewer 1 states the study shows 'the neuronal population can decode head-body angle presented across orientations, in the anterior aSTS patch (but not middle mSTS patch), except for mirror orientation.' Reviewer 2 notes 'these neurons distinguish aligned and opposite head-body configurations effectively, whereas mirror-symmetric configurations are more difficult to differentiate.' The robustness across experiments is implicitly accepted through the lack of critique.

result: Inverted bodies showed diminished decoding of head-body orientation angle compared to upright bodies, with a stronger inversion effect for zero versus straight angles than for left versus right angles. The inversion effect was consistently present for head-body configurations and less so for faces and bodies alone. This represents the first demonstration of an inversion effect for bodies with heads in the ventral bank of the STS at the single-unit level, without search bias confounds.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm this novel finding. Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'an upside-down inversion diminishes the encoding of head-body angles' as one of the three main findings. Reviewer 1 notes the study 'raises questions for future investigations comparing humans and monkeys expertise with upright and inverted configurations,' implicitly accepting the inversion effect results. No concerns are raised about the methodology or interpretation of the inversion experiments.

result: In aSTS, classification accuracies for summed head and body responses were markedly lower than for whole monkey images, and the difference between zero versus straight and left versus right angle decoding was absent for sums. In contrast, mSTS showed similar accuracies for sums and whole images, suggesting no genuine encoding of head-body angle in mSTS. This indicates that the head-body angle signal in aSTS requires the simultaneous presence of head and body.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this control analysis without critique. Reviewer 2 notes the study used 'Multiple experiments, control conditions, and detailed analyses' that 'thoroughly examined various factors that could affect the decoding results,' which would include these sum analyses. The logic of this control is not questioned by any reviewer, and it supports the main integration claims.

result: The median MSIs (multisensory integration indices) for both poses and regions were smaller than 0, indicating subadditive responses. Surprisingly, some neurons responded to either headless body or head but not to the whole monkey containing the same parts (MSI close to -1). Only a minority of neurons (4.3-6.2%) showed strong superadditive responses (MSI 0.9-1.0).
evaluation: Reviewers do not question these MSI findings. The subadditive nature of responses is implicitly accepted as part of the broader integration story. Reviewer 2's statement that neurons 'integrate head and body information in a nonlinear way' encompasses both super- and sub-additive interactions. No concerns are raised about the MSI methodology or interpretation.

result: Head-body orientation tuning generalized across poses and orientations. The same population of neurons could decode the angle between head and body irrespective of the orientation of the configuration, with marked generalization across orientations observed for P1. This generalization would not be expected if local features of individual images were employed by the classifier.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the generalization findings. Reviewer 1 notes 'using two types of body postures (sitting, standing), they show a correlation in head-body angle between postures, suggesting that monkey orientation might be more meaningful to these neurons than precise posture.' This directly supports the generalization claims. No concerns are raised about the cross-pose or cross-orientation analyses.

result: Distance matrices showed evidence for mirror-symmetric responses for lateral head and body orientations. The population of aSTS neurons showed lower sensitivity to mirror-symmetrical views for heads and bodies. Mirror symmetry may have contributed to the lower decoding of head-body angles differing only in sign, though this cannot fully explain the decoding pattern.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the mirror symmetry findings as part of the explanation for the sign-insensitivity. Reviewer 1 explicitly mentions the study's findings about 'invariance to mirror symmetry.' The authors' caveat that mirror symmetry cannot fully explain the pattern is not challenged, suggesting reviewers find the nuanced interpretation appropriate.

result: Neuron-dropping analysis for zero versus straight angle decoding in aSTS suggested less than half of neurons contributed positively. The 10 'best' neurons showed diverse tuning profiles, with at least 50% showing significant effects of head-body angle (more than expected by chance at 16%), suggesting population coding of head-body orientation angle.
evaluation: Reviewers do not critique this analysis. Reviewer 2 notes 'The decoding methods effectively and consistently revealed the encoding of head-body angles in the anterior STS neurons,' which encompasses the neuron-dropping results. The population coding interpretation aligns with reviewers' overall acceptance of the distributed encoding mechanism.

result: The highest decoding occurred for zero versus straight angles (frequent versus anatomically impossible configuration). All well-decodable angle differences consisted of possible versus impossible angles. However, no significant effect of head-body angle on mean response strength was observed, and neurons responded equally strongly to anatomically possible and impossible configurations. The anatomical possibility factor may explain better decoding for absolute angle differences, though dissociating this from mirror symmetry is not trivial.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without critique. The observation that anatomically impossible configurations elicit similar response magnitudes but can be decoded based on population patterns is implicitly accepted as part of the population coding mechanism. No reviewer questions the interpretation regarding anatomical possibility versus response strength.

result: Decoding of whole-monkey orientation was present in both mSTS and aSTS, aligning with previous studies. The decoding of head and body orientation was better in mSTS compared to aSTS, consistent with prior work.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm this finding as consistent with the literature. Reviewer 1 notes 'mSTS neurons show more specialization for head or body orientation,' which aligns with the better decoding of individual orientations in mSTS. This result is treated as confirmatory rather than novel.

result: Based on the electrophysiological data, one would predict that behavioral discrimination of head-body orientation angle would be more accurate for zero versus straight angles compared to right versus left angles, though this remains to be tested psychophysically.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes 'it's unclear how the neural representation relates to the animal's perception. Behavioural experiments using the same set of stimuli could help address this question.' This directly addresses the untested behavioral prediction. While reviewers accept the neural findings, they recognize the behavioral link remains speculative and untested.

result: Background claims establishing the research context: face and body processing are often studied separately despite natural integration; previous studies showed face-body interactions in humans and monkeys; head and body orientation are important social cues; behavioral body-inversion effects have been observed; and face-body interactions are proposed to be more prominent in anterior IT, leading to the hypothesis of stronger head-body interactions in aSTS.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the background and motivation without critique. The editor notes the study 'examines the neuronal mechanisms underlying visual perception of integrated face and body cues' using an 'innovative paradigm,' implicitly accepting the rationale. Reviewer 1 states the results 'expand prior work on the role of Anterior STS fundus face area in face-body integration,' confirming the background context.

result: Methodological details: recordings were made from fMRI-defined patches in aSTS and mSTS in two monkeys; neurons were selected based on responses to monkeys/faces/bodies versus objects; sample sizes were 98 aSTS and 100 mSTS neurons in experiment 1, and 497 aSTS and 1856 mSTS units in experiment 2; averaged responses were strongest for monkey images, followed by body and face, and weakest for objects.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the methodological approach. Reviewer 2 states 'The use of electrophysiological recordings from fMRI-defined areas elucidated the mechanism of head-body angle encoding at the level of local neuronal populations.' Reviewer 3 notes 'Combining fMRI and electrophysiology, they recorded responses of visual neurons.' The experimental design is praised as 'thoughtfully constructed and detailed' (Reviewer 2).
